supporters.quote: The estimated sleep disturbance prevalence differed significantly among measurement methods (df = 2, Q = 30.173, p < 0.001). The prevalence estimated for studies using self-report measures was 49.4 % (95 % CI: 40.4–58.4) compared with 23.7 % (95 % CI: 20.6–26.7) for studies using informant rating scales and 33.8 % (95 % CI: 24.3–43.2) for those using clinician-administered instruments
supporters.note: Mo et al. 2024, Psychiatry Res; 52 studies (44 subjective, 6 objective), 25,915 participants, 24 countries. Narrower form supported: the measurement source roughly doubles the reported prevalence of an MCI correlate (sleep disturbance among people with MCI) between studies. The paper does not estimate MCI frequency, and the measurement contrast is between studies, so it is confounded with study populations. Geographical region was at least as strong a moderator (df = 3, Q = 34.025, p < 0.001; North America 19.1% versus Oceania 45.2%, p. 12), so measurement is not 'the largest single moderator', contrary to the ledger note. Study design also separated estimates (cross-sectional 40.8% versus cohort 26.6%); sample source did not (33.5% versus 38.0%, p = 0.395, p. 11). Heterogeneity stayed above 90% (I2) inside every subgroup.

supporters.quote: Although the pooled prevalence estimates differed modestly between these subgroups (21.3 % for studies using DSM criteria vs. 28.9 % for those without clinical assessment), substantial within-group heterogeneity persisted. This pattern suggests that variability in diagnostic approach explains only part of the observed inconsistency. / Age, gender, study design and StD ascertainment also have a smaller but significant influence on the prevalence estimate compared to the previous stratifications by referral source and region.
supporters.note: Huang et al. 2026, Psychiatry Res; 52 studies, 29,321 older adults with MCI, 17 countries. Weaker form only: the case definition shifts a correlate's pooled prevalence (subthreshold depression among people with MCI) modestly, about 1.36-fold. This does not sustain 'first-order': the authors rank ascertainment below referral source and region and say the subgroup differences 'should not be interpreted as definitive'. Only 6 studies are DSM-based, against 46 that are not. No between-subgroup test statistic is reported; the p-values in Table 3 are for heterogeneity within subgroups. Referral source (hospital 36.2% versus community 21.6%) is a difference of population or setting, not of ascertainment. The paper does not estimate MCI frequency.

supporters.quote: The International Classification of Diseases (ICD) coding system was used to define MCI (ICD-10 codes: G31.8, R41, and F06.7). (p. 2) / After a median of 13.0 years of follow-up, 1797 (1.4 %) cognitively unimpaired people developed MCI (p. 3) / participants who volunteered in the UK Biobank were more health-conscious than the general population (Batty et al., 2020), which may have underestimated the incidence of MCI and dementia. (p. 8) Searched for any comparison of ascertainment methods, or of its MCI rate with other cohorts: none.
supporters.note: Wang et al. 2024, J Affect Disord; UK Biobank; 126,785 participants; Life's Essential 8 and incident MCI or dementia. Uses a single ascertainment method (ICD-10 codes plus adjudicated records) and reports cumulative incidence, not prevalence. Its only comment on the low rate attributes it to healthy-volunteer selection, a population factor, not to ascertainment. The ascertainment contrast exists only in the ledger's juxtaposition of this study with others. Internal inconsistency: the incident-MCI counts in Table 1 (592 women plus 833 men, 1,425) do not match the 1,797 given in the text. P-648 and P-650 use the same dataset.

supporters.quote: The International Classification of Diseases 10th revision (ICD-10) F06.7, G31.8 and R41 codes were used to identify participants with MCI if one or more of these codes were recorded as a primary or secondary diagnosis in the health records. (p. 3) / (Table 2) Low 377 (2.00) / Normal 2390 (1.54) / High 505 (1.88) (p. 5) Searched for any comparison of MCI ascertainment, or any comment on the MCI rate: none.
supporters.note: Zhang et al. 2025, J Affect Disord; UK Biobank; 200,726 participants; birth weight, midlife obesity and MCI. The ledger's 1.6% can be derived from Table 2 (3,272 of 200,726) but the paper never states it, compares it or comments on it. The paper's only definitional contrast concerns an exposure: central obesity is 31.99% of the sample by waist circumference and 43.59% by waist-to-hip ratio, with almost identical hazard ratios for MCI (1.25 and 1.27), and the authors stress the 'consistency in results'. That is not an MCI estimate, and if anything it shows the association is robust to the definition. Same dataset as P-648, so not an independent source.

supporters.quote: Observed Baseline scores were comparable to Observed One-Year Follow-up scores for the vast majority of RBANS Index scores. (p. 8) / Z scores for the clinic amnestic MCI sample were lower than zero for all 5 RBANS Indexes and the Total Scale score. (p. 9) / These findings are consistent with the literature suggesting that the use of SRB prediction equations can be more sensitive to change over time than the traditional baseline versus follow-up assessment method (p. 11)
supporters.note: Hammers et al. 2022, Clin Neuropsychol; Utah; amnestic MCI, 64 recruited from the community and 58 from a clinic; RBANS given twice, one year apart. Narrower form supported: in the same MCI samples, the change-scoring method decides whether decline is reported. Raw baseline-to-follow-up comparison shows mostly no change, while standardised regression-based scoring shows decline below expectation, with 47% 'declined' on the memory indexes in the clinic sample (p. 10). This is method-dependence of a decline estimate within MCI, not of MCI frequency. The authors concede that over-prediction at low baseline scores (regression to the mean) may create apparent declines (p. 15). The clinic-versus-community difference is about recruitment (population), not ascertainment. Samples are small and 98 to 100% Caucasian.

supporters.quote: The MCI group showed declines between 1.6% and 29.1%. (p. 1) Searched for any comparison of two ascertainment methods for the same quantity, or of MCI frequency by definition: none; every decline estimate uses one reliable-change method against one healthy-control group.
supporters.note: Garcia Rosas et al. 2021, Wien Klin Wochenschr; Vienna memory clinic; 358 patients (270 MCI); Neuropsychological Test Battery Vienna scored with the reliable change index. The 1.6% to 29.1% range spans different subtests, and so different cognitive domains (for example 1.6% on phonemic fluency against 29.1% on the Boston Naming Test). The spread reflects which function is measured, not how one quantity is ascertained. The conversion table (MCI to SCD 14.4%, MCI to AD 17.8%) is not analysed as an ascertainment effect. Short report, single clinic.

supporters.quote: Transition rates after 3 years are between 5.9% (InDDEx) and 46.4% (NACC), both with a standard error of 1.1%. (p. 7) / It will be noted that there are wide differences between the five samples with regard to almost all inclusion and exclusion criteria. (p. 4) / Whatever the reasons for the varying transition rates in these mostly company-sponsored trials are, it is obvious that the MCI criteria available some 20 years ago were not sufficiently precise to allow selection of clinically homogeneous and internationally comparable MCI patient groups. (p. 9)
supporters.note: Berres, Monsch and Spiegel 2021, Alzheimers Res Ther; five MCI datasets (ADNI n = 395, NACC 4,328, the InDDEx trial 831, CNG 726, BS-MC 1,558). Narrower form supported: samples defined by different MCI criteria report roughly eightfold differences in three-year progression, and the authors attribute this to imprecise MCI criteria. The case definition is confounded with setting (a drug trial against cohorts and memory clinics), geography, dementia ascertainment and three-year attrition, which ranges from 25% to 98%. The estimate is progression among people already diagnosed with MCI, not MCI frequency. The remark that MCI incidence and prevalence estimates vary widely is cited from others (Ward et al.; Han et al.), not a result of this paper.

supporters.quote: MCI rates by consensus, actuarial criteria, and LCA were 44%, 53%, and 41%, respectively. (p. 1) / Thus, while the choice of diagnostic method had a small impact on MCI prevalence among White participants (from 46% to 52%), Black participants were twice as likely to be classified as having MCI using the actuarial approach (54%) than using consensus or LCA (27–30%). (p. 8)
supporters.note: Devlin et al. 2022, J Alzheimers Dis; Penn Alzheimer's Disease Research Center; N = 354 (68% White, 29% Black). Three case definitions applied to the same sample: MCI frequency is 41% to 53% overall (a 12-point spread), 46% to 52% in White participants (which the authors call a 'small impact'), and two-fold in Black participants (27 to 30% against 54%). This supports the row's 'few percentage points within a single sample' end, plus a two-fold shift within a subgroup. Limits: research-centre sample restricted at entry to consensus-diagnosed normal cognition or MCI; highly educated; the actuarial rule (1 SD cut-off, 14 tests in six domains) is more liberal than in earlier applications, and the authors note this raises the number of MCI classifications.

supporters.quote: We explored but discounted the use of an alternative criterion of 1.0 SD below an adjusted mean because this yielded implausibly large MCI categories. (p. 6) / The prevalence of MCI in ABC21 was 15/178 (8.4%) at an age of about 77y and was 39/425 (9.2%) at age of about 64y in ABC36. [...] We consider the differences between the studies in terms of procedures to adjust cognitive scores for the effects of sex, childhood IQ and education to be the likely source of these differences (p. 8)
supporters.note: Whalley et al. 2022, Brain Sci; Aberdeen 1921 and 1936 birth cohorts; MCI defined by psychometric criteria alone. The support is qualitative only. The prevalence under the 1.0 SD threshold is not reported and the Lothian comparison figures are not given, so the paper gives no magnitude; attributing the Lothian difference to score-adjustment procedures is the authors' untested interpretation. Its psychometric-only classifications were highly unstable (18 of 27 amnestic MCI cases in ABC36 no longer met the criteria at the second assessment, p. 12). Weaker form: the authors report, without figures, that the impairment threshold and the score-adjustment procedure change psychometric MCI prevalence.

supporters.quote: Accounting for PEs increased MCI prevalence at follow-up by 9.2% (272 vs. 249 MCI), and reduced reversion to normal by 28.8% (57 vs. 80 reverters). (p. 1) / The overall reversion rate (i.e., being classified as CN at follow-up) was 24.3% (n = 80) using PE-unadjusted scores and 17.3% (n = 57) using PE-adjusted scores. (p. 5)
supporters.note: Sanderson-Cimino et al. 2022, Front Aging Neurosci; ADNI; 329 participants with MCI at baseline (Jak-Bondi criteria) who returned at one year. The sample and criteria are the same and only the scoring procedure differs (with or without practice-effect adjustment): MCI at follow-up is 249 against 272 of 329 (75.7% against 82.7%, a 7-point shift and a 9.2% relative change). This supports the row's 'few percentage points within a single sample' end. Limits: the figure is the proportion retaining an MCI classification among baseline-MCI returnees (highly educated ADNI volunteers), not population prevalence; practice effects were estimated with a bootstrap pseudo-replacement design.

supporters.quote: In our sample, the prevalence of MCI among patients with metabolic risks was as high as 82.7 percent. (p. 6) / First, the diagnosis of MCI was based solely on the questionnaire. (p. 8) Searched for any comparison of ascertainment methods: none. The authors explain the high figure by the population: similar to the results of recent studies showing that the prevalence of MCI in individuals with metabolic risk factors was approximately between 65 and 75 percent (p. 6).
supporters.note: Buawangpong et al. 2022, Healthcare; Chiang Mai hospital outpatients with metabolic risk factors; N = 421; MCI defined as MoCA below 25. The paper uses a single cut-off. Its high MCI frequency is confounded with a selected clinical population, and the authors attribute it to that population, not to ascertainment. Any ascertainment contrast is the ledger's, built across studies.

supporters.quote: (Table 1, 2017-2019) MCI Observed rate 0.015 / Expected rate 0.196 / Detection rate 0.079 (p. 4) / Only 7.9% of expected MCI cases have been diagnosed in the most recently available data covering 2017 to 2019. (p. 5) / Based on the original CCW algorithm, the observed rate would have been 0.106 and the detection rate 1.23, suggesting a 23% rate of overdiagnosis. (p. 6)
supporters.note: Mattke et al. 2023, Alzheimers Res Ther; the full US Medicare population aged 65 and over, 2015 to 2019 (about 41 million people), with expected rates from the Health and Retirement Study. In the same population, claims-coded MCI (ICD-10 G31.84, two claims) is about 1.5%, against about 20% from classification by cognitive assessment (the HRS Langa-Kabeto-Weir method, projected onto Medicare with a demographic probit model, AUC 0.67): a gap of roughly thirteen-fold. The choice of dementia coding algorithm alone moves the observed dementia rate from 0.095 to 0.106. This supports the several-fold end of the row, shown within one population rather than between studies. Limits: the authors read the MCI gap as under-detection rather than measurement artefact; the expected rate is a model projection, not a measurement in the same individuals, and rests on cognitive scores, 'not the same as a true clinical diagnosis'; industry funded (Genentech).

reasoning: Three supporters show, in their own data, that how MCI is ascertained moves the estimate of MCI frequency. P-955: in the same sample, consensus diagnosis gives 44%, actuarial criteria 53% and latent class analysis 41%; the spread is 46 to 52% in White participants and 27 to 30% against 54% in Black participants. P-971: with the same ADNI sample and criteria, practice-effect adjustment moves MCI at follow-up from 249 to 272 of 329 and reversion from 24.3% to 17.3%. P-1046: in the same Medicare population, claims-coded MCI is 0.015 against an expected 0.196 from cognitive assessment. They come from three distinct datasets (Penn ADRC, ADNI, Medicare with HRS) and three method families (diagnostic-algorithm comparison, score adjustment, records against assessment), so the row holds as worded: a few to about twelve percentage points within one sample, two-fold within a subgroup, and an order of magnitude between records-based and assessment-based sources. Five supporters answer partly. P-654 and P-657 concern the prevalence of correlates (sleep disturbance, subthreshold depression) among people with MCI, not MCI frequency, and in both the ascertainment moderator is matched or outranked: in P-654, region has Q 34.0 against 30.2 for measurement; in P-657, the authors rank ascertainment below referral source and region and call its effect (21.3% against 28.9%) modest. P-924 shows the change-scoring method decides whether decline is detected in MCI. P-937 shows about eightfold differences in progression across differently defined MCI samples, confounded with setting and attrition. P-962 reports, without figures, that a 1.0 SD threshold gave 'implausibly large' MCI categories. Four answer no. P-648 and P-650 report ICD-coded UK Biobank incidence with no comparison, and P-648 attributes its low rate to healthy-volunteer selection. P-926's 1.6 to 29.1% range spans different cognitive domains. P-982 uses a single MoCA cut-off and attributes its high rate to its metabolic-risk population. Four corrections follow. First, the cross-study contrast in the ledger notes (UK Biobank's 1.4 to 1.6% incidence against 17.3 to 65.2% cross-sectional prevalence) is the ledger's own juxtaposition, not a result any of those papers reports; the several-fold end should be cited to P-1046. Second, the supporter count of 12 in the Table A1 row should fall to 3 (yes only) or 8 (yes or partly), and P-648 and P-650 share one dataset. Third, the ledger statement's stronger claims (a 'factor of two or more' in general; ascertainment 'dominates every substantive moderator tested alongside it') are not supported: in P-654 region is as strong a moderator as measurement, P-657 ranks ascertainment as secondary, and P-955 calls the method effect small among White participants. The Table A1 narrowing is therefore needed and correct. Fourth, a tighter wording that cites only the supporters carrying it would be: 'Ascertainment moves estimates of MCI frequency: by a few to about twelve percentage points between diagnostic methods or scoring procedures applied to the same sample (P-955, P-971), up to two-fold within a subgroup (P-955), and by an order of magnitude between records-based diagnosis and assessment-based classification in the same population (P-1046).'
